newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian magistrates stop work to protest attacks.
newsitem.headline: Belgian magistrates stop work to protest attacks.

text.p: Belgian magistrates stopped work for a symbolic 15 minutes on Tuesday in protest at what they see as deeply unjust accusations of incompetence in the country's paedophile kidnapping, abuse and murder scandals.

Their anger, which threatens to undermine efforts to reform Belgium's antiquated justice and police systems, has developed into a war of words between the magistrates and politicians, particularly Justice Minister Stefaan De Clerck.

The magistrates stopped work at 10.30 a.m. and held meetings to demonstrate against an official report accusing them of sloth and lack of professionalism in their handling of the spate of child disappearances.
It was the first strike by the magistrates since 1989.

The report, approved unanimously by parliament two weeks ago, said at least two of the five young girls found dead since last August might have been rescued if police and magistrates had spent more time working with rather than against each other.
In particular it accused Brussels Public Prosecutor Benoit Dejemeppe of being incapable, prompting De Clerck to ask him to resign or at least step aside.

But Dejemeppe, supported by his staff, has refused to go, and the magistrates -- overworked and under-resourced -- have threatened to reopen the hundreds of dormant missing persons files they have been unable to tackle due to lack of personnel.

The Brussels magistrates accuse De Clerck of having for years ignored their pleas for more resources, and contributing to the problem by insisting that any new appointments be fluent in both French and Dutch -- the two languages of the capital city.
The fight prompted one member of the parliamentary commission which conducted the report to lash out.

"If the magistrates had been as energetic in their efforts to find the children as they are in defending themselves, we wouldn't be here," Flemish Socialist Party member Renaat Landuyt said at the weekend.
The commission report, which followed six months of hearings that riveted the nation, spared no one in its description of the shambolic investigations into the child kidnappings, rapes and murders.
Police have found the bodies of eight-year-olds Julie Lejeune, Melissa Russo and Loubna Benaissa as well as those of teenagers An Marchal and Eefje Lambrecks, and they are still looking for more.
Two convicted child rapists -- Marc Dutroux and Patrick Derochette -- have been charged with murder.
The all-party report made recommendations ranging from creation of a single police force to replace the existing three rival forces, to reform of the whole justice system.
But it also said that sheer incompetence might not have been the only answer to the failed investigations.

The commission will continue its work until the end of September to try to give substance to its theory that Dutroux and Derochette and their accomplices might have escaped arrest earlier because they had high level protection.
In October more than 250,000 people marched through Brussels to show support for the victims and demonstrate their disgust at a system seen as at best incompetent and at worse as corrupt.
